newsitem.title: USA: NYC says PaineWebber settles case for $3.3 mln.
newsitem.headline: NYC says PaineWebber settles case for $3.3 mln.

text.p: New York City said on Monday that PaineWebber had agreed to pay it about $3.3 million to settle a back tax case. This worked out to nearly half the approximately $7.2 million sum the city said it was owed.

"There was a dispute (for tax years 1982 to 1985), and as we do in many cases, both sides settled the amount they would pay," said Paul Rephen, senior assistant corporation counsel for the City of New York. He added the city late last week got a check from the brokerage house.

PaineWebber earlier said it settled the case, but did not disclose any details. "PaineWebber is pleased to have reached an amicable settlement with the City of New York, which has agreed to drop its appeal," the company said in a statement prepared in answer to a question about the matter.

The city official explained the case arose out of a corporate tax audit for the years 1982 to 1985. The New York Post in mid-February said that the city stood to lose the $7.2 million it said the firm owed because it had missed a deadline by one day. A city tax judge had ruled in favor of the brokerage house, a decision New York City then appealed.

Rephen declined to speculate about PaineWebber's motives in choosing to settle the case. City officials previously said that the dispute might have snarled the company's campaign to keep underwriting New York City's debt.

The city is in the midst of picking underwriters for its new borrowing arm, the New York City Transitional Financing Authority, and for the first time, it took steps to ensure that firms and their top managers have good track records in all their dealings with the city.

Underwriters compete fiercely for the top and most lucrative spots on the syndicates, and the city has said it might have to reshuffle its present teams as a result of the new bankers it was expected to pick in May or June.
PaineWebber now serves on the syndicate that sells New York City Municipal Water Finance Authority bonds, a team that plans to sell about $640 million of debt on Tuesday.
